notes.meaning: Before the fighting began, the leaders of Israel made a rash promise at Mizpah, swearing that no one would let his daughter marry a Benjamite. They treated their fellow Israelites like dangerous pagans because of the wicked crime at Gibeah. This hasty oath trapped them later when the war was over and Benjamin faced total ruin.

The people gathered at Bethel before the ark of God and sat weeping until evening. Their hot anger had cooled, and their great victory now felt like an awful tragedy. Looking back on the terrible slaughter of their own brothers filled them with deep sorrow.

The Israelites cried out in grief, asking God why a whole tribe was now missing from the nation. They had nearly wiped out the family of Benjamin themselves, yet their question sounded like they were blaming God instead of their own violent fury. The twelve tribes were meant to stand together as one united family under God's covenant, which was His special agreement with them.

Early the next morning, the people built an altar and presented burnt offerings and peace offerings to God. A new altar was likely needed because of the huge number of sacrifices brought by the vast crowd. Even while worshiping, they struggled to figure out how to repair the damage their anger had caused.

The leaders recalled an earlier oath that anyone who refused to assemble at Mizpah to oppose evil must be put to death. They hoped this strict rule might also help them find wives for Benjamin without breaking their other vow. In their distress, they looked for legal loopholes rather than admitting their foolish choices.

The people felt deep sorrow for their brother tribe Benjamin because a whole branch of Israel was on the brink of extinction. Only six hundred fighting men of Benjamin had survived by hiding on a rocky crag, while all their women and children had been killed. Losing a full twelfth of the nation was a disaster the other tribes could hardly bear.

The leaders debated how to find wives for the surviving men so the family line of Benjamin would not die out. They could not give their own daughters because they had bound themselves with a solemn oath in the Lord's name. They felt hopelessly trapped between watching a tribe disappear and breaking a sacred vow.

The assembly asked whether any town in Israel had failed to report to the gathering before the Lord at Mizpah. A review showed that no one from the city of Jabesh-gilead had attended the national meeting. Because Jabesh-gilead had stayed away, its people had not taken the vow forbidding marriage to Benjamin.

The leaders took an official roll call of the entire assembly to confirm that the report was accurate. The count verified that not a single resident from Jabesh-gilead was present in the camp. Their absence marked them for severe punishment under Israel's earlier oath.

The assembly sent twelve thousand brave soldiers across the Jordan River to Jabesh-gilead. Their orders were to strike the town with the sword, killing the men, women, and children. To fix the near-destruction of one tribe, they turned to slaughtering another group of their own countrymen.

The soldiers were commanded to place the city under a ban, devoting to destruction every male and every married woman. Devoting to destruction meant setting people or things apart for complete death under divine judgment. Israel copied the rules of war usually reserved for pagan enemies and applied them ruthlessly to fellow Israelites.

The raiding army spared four hundred young women in Jabesh-gilead who were unmarried virgins. They brought them back as captives to the main camp at Shiloh. The leaders intended to use these surviving young women as forced brides for the Benjamite refugees.

The leaders of Israel sent messengers to the six hundred Benjamite men hiding at the rock of Rimmon. They proclaimed terms of peace and assured them they would not be harmed. This allowed the frightened survivors to come out of hiding without fear of further attacks.

The surviving Benjamites returned from their stronghold and received the four hundred young women saved from Jabesh-gilead. The leaders assumed they had kept their own oath because these women came from a town that had not joined the vow. Even after this brutal massacre, there were still two hundred Benjamites left without wives.

The Israelites continued to mourn over Benjamin because a painful void remained in the family of tribes. Scripture states that the Lord had made this gap because He permitted their civil war and harsh punishment to take place. Human attempts to fix sinful blunders only created more heartache and shortage.

The elders met in council again to find a solution for the remaining two hundred men. All the original women of Benjamin had been destroyed in the fighting, leaving no local brides. The leaders had closed the door to giving their own daughters because of their sworn promise.

The leaders agreed that the survivors must keep their ancestral land so that a whole tribe would not vanish from Israel. Under God's law, tribal territories belonged permanently to each assigned tribe and could not be handed over to others. Finding wives for the remaining men was the only way to raise up children to care for the land.

The leaders repeated that none of the assembled Israelites could give their own daughters as wives to Benjamin. They had pronounced a solemn curse upon anyone who broke that promise. They cared deeply about the outward letter of their oath, even while planning another morally corrupt scheme.

The elders remembered that an annual festival to the Lord was about to take place at Shiloh. The passage carefully describes the exact location of Shiloh, north of Bethel and east of the road leading to Shechem. This religious gathering provided the backdrop they needed for their next plan.

The elders instructed the two hundred Benjamites who still needed wives to travel to Shiloh and hide in the nearby vineyards. The thick grapevines provided ideal cover where the men could conceal themselves unseen. This plan was secretly arranged by the elders rather than by seeking direction from God.

The men were told to wait until the young women of Shiloh came out into the open fields to perform religious dances for the feast. As the women danced alone away from the town, each Benjamite was to rush out, seize one for himself, and carry her away to his own territory. This abduction allowed the elders to claim that no father had willingly given his daughter away.

The elders promised to step in if the fathers or brothers came to complain about the kidnapping of their daughters. They planned to ask for mercy on behalf of the Benjamites, arguing that the families bore no guilt because they had not voluntarily given the brides away. It was a clever excuse designed to calm family anger while dodging religious guilt.

The two hundred Benjamites carried out the plan, seizing the dancing women and taking them home. Each man took one wife, and the survivors returned to their tribal lands to rebuild their ruined towns. Although the tribe was preserved from total ruin, the methods used revealed how deeply the nation had fallen into disorder.

Once the crisis had ended and the Benjamites were settled, the rest of the Israelite army disbanded. Every man returned home to his own clan and his inherited family property. The tribes pulled through the ordeal, but the nation was left deeply wounded by its civil war.

The book closes with the solemn reminder that Israel had no king during those dark years. Without godly leadership to enforce God's law, every person simply did whatever seemed right to them. This widespread lawlessness pointed ahead to the nation's urgent need for a righteous king to guide them.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars argue that the negative portrayal of Benjamin at the close of Judges was designed to highlight the failures of Saul's tribe and support the rise of David's royal line.
